source.title: AdvPrefix: An Objective for Nuanced LLM Jailbreaks
source.authors: Sicheng Zhu; Brandon Amos; Yuandong Tian; Chuan Guo; I. Evtimov

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. The text identifies the paper as a NeurIPS 2025 paper, despite the supplied venue metadata.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether attacks that elicit response prefixes can bypass safety behavior, using optimized jailbreak prompts and measured harmful-completion success rates. It does not test the original studies’ fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.gate_note: The paper reports jailbreak success rates for prefix-forcing attacks and a prefilling result. These bear on V4. It does not report fine-tuning effects, per-token KL, weight localization, why safety is shallow, or safety-deepening training results. Other judges’ results are reported as an evaluation ablation, not separate outcomes of the safety-bypass behavior cataloged here.
record.test_reason: The study measures how often four safety-tuned chat models give complete, faithful harmful responses when attacks force a response opening (suffix or full-prompt optimization toward a target prefix) or when that opening is prefilled. This bears directly on V4 by a different method than the originals. It runs no fine-tuning, per-token KL, weight-localization or deepening-training experiments.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that the standard 'Sure, here is' prefix-forcing objective is misspecified: eliciting or prefilling the prefix does not ensure a complete, faithful harmful response, because newer models self-correct. It is also overconstrained. Model-specific prefixes chosen for high prefilling ASR and low NLL sharply raise nuanced ASR. Hence newer models' deeper alignment can be bypassed and does not generalize to unseen prefixes.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates optimized jailbreak prompts and prefix prefilling, not fine-tuning on harmful or benign examples or aligned-versus-base tokenwise KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with victim model, attack method, prefix objective, suffix length, and whether the full prompt or only a suffix is optimized. The original prefilled opening removes direct refusals but does not ensure a complete and faithful harmful response.

fits_no_version.finding: Newer models (Llama-3, Llama-3.1, Gemma-2) often emit the forced affirmative opening and then self-correct, whereas Llama-2 refuses directly. This apparent 'deeper' alignment does not generalize to model-specific prefixes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deeper alignment observed in deployed models (recovery after a harmful opening) is specific to the openings seen in training and fails on unseen compliant prefixes.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025), as stated in the paper text
record.problems: The text reports ASRs averaged over four independent runs and across requests but gives no uncertainty estimates. The prefilling outcome is shown in a figure without numeric values stated in the text. The authors note that their prefix-selection pipeline has computational cost and that the objective requires target-model log probabilities.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1 and Table 2 also give direct-refusal, incomplete, and unfaithful failure-category percentages. Those breakdowns were not separately rowed here; the retained rows catalog the reported nuanced jailbreak success measure and the distinct prefilling result.

untested.parts: Decoding changes (e.g. sampling or temperature attacks). No no-attack baseline rate of harmful compliance is given.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models: not measured.
Causes of shallowness: not studied. The authors only speculate that developers train on the 'Sure, here is' prefixes.
Deepening training: not performed. Newer models' self-correction is observed, but their training is unknown.

missing.what: Failure breakdown of the original objective by final loss: lower loss removes refusals, but overall failure stays above 80%.
The same attacks scored by HarmBench, JailbreakBench and StrongReject, showing judge-dependent ASR (e.g. Gemma-2 original: 7.4 vs 21.5).
Meta-evaluation: existing judges overestimate ASR (about 10% true vs nearly 40% on Gemma-2).
Harmfulness win rate against an uncensored LLM: about 10% for the original objective vs 30–50% for AdvPrefix.
Reasoning model (R1-distilled-Llama-3-8B): default prefixes fail; model-specific prefixes succeed. Figure only.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily an attack-objective paper. Its AdvPrefix vs Original comparisons are method comparisons, but the absolute success rates under forced or prefilled openings bear on V4. No no-attack baseline is reported, and results are averaged over four runs with no uncertainty. The key V4-relevant nuance: on newer models, generic prefilling or forcing defeats direct refusal but not harmful completion. This differs from the original sources' Llama-2 and Gemma-1 prefilling results. The selected prefixes depend on the nuanced judge, which is also the evaluator.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning and its effect on refusal.
Benign fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models.
The paper tests optimized suffix/full-prompt attacks using response prefixes and reports a prefilling result. It does not test decoding changes.
Localization of safety behavior in weights or ranks.
Whether training data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and its durability.
